```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.2, dpi = 150, out.width = "100%")
ia <- requireNamespace("ggiraph", quietly = TRUE) && knitr::is_html_output()
pandoc <- rmarkdown::pandoc_available()
```

An analysis ends in a manuscript, a report, a slide or a web page. This
vignette shows how the tables and figures of a joinpoint fit get there:
saved to files in the format each needs, written into a complete report,
printed in R Markdown and Quarto documents, and drawn as interactive
graphics.

The examples use the tuberculosis and stroke mortality of `us_mortality`:

```{r}
library(joinpoint)
fit <- joinpoint(subset(us_mortality, cause %in% c("Stroke", "Tuberculosis")),
                 year, rate, by = "cause", kmax = 3, ci_method = "parametric")
dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "joinpoint-reports")
dir.create(dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
```

## Tables

`jp_save()` writes a table in the format given by the extension of the file:
`.csv`, `.tsv` and `.txt` for spreadsheets and other software, `.md` for
Markdown, `.tex` for LaTeX, and `.docx`, `.odt`, `.rtf`, `.pptx`, `.html`
and `.pdf` for documents. A title becomes the caption, and a note is printed
under the table:

```{r}
tab <- jp_table(fit)
jp_save(tab, file.path(dir, "trends.tex"), title = "Trends in mortality",
        note = "* The APC or AAPC differs from 0 at alpha = 0.05.",
        label = "tab:trends")
```

The LaTeX table uses the rules of the booktabs package
(`\usepackage{booktabs}` in the preamble) and escapes the special
characters of LaTeX:

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(readLines(file.path(dir, "trends.tex")), sep = "\n")
```

Any data frame can be saved this way, for example the APCs as numbers or
the model selection statistics, with the decimals set by `digits`:

```{r}
jp_save(apc(fit), file.path(dir, "apc.csv"))
jp_save(model_selection(fit)$criteria, file.path(dir, "selection.md"),
        digits = 2)
```

Word, OpenDocument, PowerPoint, RTF, HTML and PDF documents are made with
Pandoc, which comes with RStudio and Quarto, through the rmarkdown package;
PDF documents also need LaTeX (for example `tinytex::install_tinytex()`).
A Word table for a manuscript:

```{r, eval = pandoc}
jp_save(tab, file.path(dir, "trends.docx"), title = "Trends in mortality")
```

## Figures

Figures are saved the same way: in the image formats of `ggsave()` (`.png`,
`.pdf`, `.svg`, `.tiff`, `.eps` and others), as a LaTeX figure, or inside a
Word, OpenDocument, PowerPoint or HTML document. `width`, `height` (inches)
and `dpi` set the size and resolution:

```{r}
g <- autoplot(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE)
jp_save(g, file.path(dir, "trends.png"), width = 7, height = 4, dpi = 300)
jp_save(g, file.path(dir, "trends.tex"), title = "Mortality trends",
        label = "fig:trends")
```

The `.tex` file is a `figure` environment that includes a PDF of the
figure written beside it (`trends.pdf`), ready for `\input{}` in a
manuscript.

## Complete reports

`jp_report()` writes the whole analysis: the settings in words, the table of
APCs and AAPCs, the joinpoints, the model selection statistics and the
figures. An `.Rmd` or `.qmd` file gives the R Markdown or Quarto source,
with the fit saved beside it, ready to edit and render:

```{r}
jp_report(fit, file.path(dir, "mortality.qmd"),
          title = "Trends in mortality", author = "A. Analyst")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, comment = ""}
cat(head(readLines(file.path(dir, "mortality.qmd")), 32), sep = "\n")
```

Other extensions give the rendered report: `.html`, `.docx`, `.odt`,
`.pdf`, `.md` or `.tex`. The figures of HTML reports are interactive when
the ggiraph package is installed.

```{r, eval = pandoc}
jp_report(fit, file.path(dir, "mortality.docx"), title = "Trends in mortality")
```

`jp_save()` of a fit writes the same report.

## Fits in R Markdown and Quarto documents

A fit printed in a chunk of an R Markdown or Quarto document shows the same
summary as in the console. With the option `joinpoint.knit_table`, set once
in the first chunk of the document, it appears instead as the table of
`jp_table()`, formatted for the output (HTML, LaTeX, Word or Markdown); the
chunk option `tab.cap` sets its caption:

```{r, include = FALSE}
old <- options(joinpoint.knit_table = NULL)
```

```{r, tab.cap = "Trends in stroke and tuberculosis mortality."}
options(joinpoint.knit_table = TRUE)
fit
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
options(old)
```

Figures are drawn by `autoplot()` and the other plot functions as in any
chunk.

## Interactive graphics

The trend figure (`autoplot()`), the APC and AAPC figures (`plot_apc()`,
`plot_aapc()`) and the model selection figure (`plot_selection()`) can be
drawn as interactive graphics, with `interactive = TRUE` in the plot
function and `jp_interactive()`, or `jp_interactive()` on the fit
directly, with `plot` choosing the figure. The graphic looks like the static
figure. Hovering a segment shows its period, APC, confidence interval and
p value and highlights the segment with its band and label; hovering an
observation shows its value, its confidence interval and the fitted trend;
hovering a joinpoint shows its location and confidence interval. The
toolbar zooms and saves the graphic as an image.

```{r, eval = ia}
jp_interactive(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE, height = 4.2)
```

```{r, eval = !ia, echo = FALSE, fig.alt = "Stroke and tuberculosis mortality from 1900 to 1998 on a logarithmic axis, with the fitted joinpoint models colored by trend direction."}
autoplot(fit, color_by = "trend", log_y = TRUE)
```

The other figures are chosen with `plot`, here the APC of each segment:

```{r, eval = ia}
jp_interactive(fit, plot = "apc", height = 3.5)
```

A figure changed with the grammar of ggplot2 stays interactive:

```{r, eval = ia}
g <- autoplot(fit, interactive = TRUE) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Mortality per 100,000", x = NULL)
jp_interactive(g, height = 4.2)
```

The graphics are htmlwidgets: they appear in the RStudio viewer, in HTML
documents made with R Markdown or Quarto, on pkgdown sites and in Shiny
applications (with `ggiraph::girafeOutput()` and `ggiraph::renderGirafe()`),
and `jp_save()` writes them to a standalone web page (without Pandoc, the
page needs the folder of scripts written beside it):

```{r, eval = ia}
jp_save(jp_interactive(fit), file.path(dir, "mortality.html"))
```

By default the text of the graphic uses fonts found on the computer that
opens it, which keeps the page small; `embed_fonts = TRUE` embeds the
fonts, so that the graphic looks exactly the same everywhere, at the cost
of several megabytes.

```{r cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(dir, recursive = TRUE)
```
